title: Punk Band Guitar Wolf Rocks Back Into Takeuchi Tetsuro’s ‘Wild Zero Overdrive’ at Tokyo Gap-Financing Market
description: Guitar Wolf, a real-life punk outfit with a long record of touring internationally, headlines “Wild Zero Overdrive,” director Takeuchi Tetsuro’s fo
body:
Guitar Wolf, a real-life punk outfit with a long record of touring internationally, headlines “Wild Zero Overdrive,” director Takeuchi Tetsuro’s follow-up to his 1999 film “Wild Zero.” 

	The project is among those at this year’s Tokyo Gap-Financing Market.

	Takeuchi said he is using the original as a template and updating it for the present day. “Precisely because we’re living in the age of AI, I want to convey the heat that comes from raw, primal punk rock,” Takeuchi said.
	

	The Japan-Canada project is produced by Takegei Company Limited. Takeuchi is putting together the budget with his own money as the base, while also searching for distribution partners. Casting is underway.

	“Rock’n’roll never dies. And love for Japanese subculture and rock’n’roll. UFOs. Motorcycles. Love,” Takeuchi said of what he wants audiences to take from the film.

	“I’ve been a huge fan of ‘Wild Zero’ (1999) ever since it came out. I even named my dog Ace, after the film’s main character.” said Toronto-based producer Takabatake Aki.

	Takabatake met the new film’s cinematographer by chance in Toronto, while Takabatake was working on a commercial, and took the encounter as a sign.

	“‘Wild Zero Overdrive’ and I are bound together by an unbreakable rock ’n’ roll pact,” Takabatake said.

	In Tokyo, the team will pitch the project to industry professionals at TGFM / Frontières Tokyo. The producers are also looking for further financing, distributors in Japan and abroad, and international sales agents.

	“Hopefully, we’ll be able to connect with some great potential partners who share our passion for the project,” Takabatake said.
	

	The Tokyo Gap-Financing Market runs as part of TIFFCOM, the content market attached to the Tokyo International Film Festival.

title: Acrobatic Pastor’s Secret Obsession Drives Boo Junfeng’s ‘Trinity’ at Tokyo Gap-Financing Market
description: A celebrity preacher who performs daredevil stunts for his congregation while hiding his fixation on a young follower sits at the center of “Trinit
body:
A celebrity preacher who performs daredevil stunts for his congregation while hiding his fixation on a young follower sits at the center of “Trinity,” the new feature from director Boo Junfeng, which is among the projects at this year’s Tokyo Gap-Financing Market.

	Structured in three chapters modeled on the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, the film follows Johnny, a pastor from Taiwan whose sermons have built him a large Singaporean following at a popular megachurch. The faithful also turn out in large numbers for the elaborate acrobatic shows he stages in the vein of Cirque du Soleil.
	

	Though publicly known for his conservative stance, Johnny grows infatuated with Yang, a newcomer to his training program, and his preferential treatment of the young man soon becomes hard to miss. It unsettles his wife Ruth, and David, his leading disciple and his daughter’s husband-to-be, both of whom share in running the church.

	When Yang vanishes, a frantic Johnny starts his own inquiry. The clues point toward the people in his inner circle, with tragic results. Johnny and Ruth later relocate to rural Taiwan, where they keep a low profile and worship at a modest local congregation – until Johnny glimpses an enigmatic stranger who may yet bring the couple divine grace.

	“I’ve always been very interested in the subject of sexuality and faith, and I wanted to make a film that dives deep into the psyche of these characters within a church,” Boo said.

	Boo, a Singaporean filmmaker, made his feature debut with “Sandcastle” (2010), which became the first film from Singapore to be selected for Cannes Critics’ Week. His follow-up, capital punishment drama “Apprentice,” played in Cannes’ Un Certain Regard section in 2016. He has also served as creative director of Singapore’s National Day Parade, including the 2025 edition marking the country’s 60th anniversary, and currently serves as chair of the Singapore International Film Festival.
	

	Producer Raymond Phathanavirangoon, whose credits include “Apprentice,” co-wrote “Trinity” with Boo and has been involved since the idea first took shape. He has also produced Pen-ek Ratanaruang’s “Headshot,” Ron Howard’s “Thirteen Lives” and Pang Ho-Cheung’s “Dream Home” and “Aberdeen.” His earlier career included stints as an international programmer for the Toronto International Film Festival and a program delegate for Cannes Critics’ Week, and he co-founded the Southeast Asia Fiction Film Lab (SEAFIC).

	“Personally, I have had people close to me convert to Christianity due to Evangelism, but this is seldom seen in Asian films,” Phathanavirangoon said.

	He added that the way some Asian churches build spectacle into their services is what sets the story apart. “Some are surprised that churches can host Cirque du Soleil-style performances like in our film, but just earlier this year in Korea, a stunt sent a man dressed as Jesus into the sky, and that went super viral.”

	“Trinity” is now in post-production. Both Boo and Phathanavirangoon said the team is coming to Tokyo with a small gap in its financing left to close before the film can be completed.

	“I hope people will empathize with the characters, despite them being flawed human beings,” Boo said.

	The project is produced by Peanut Pictures, Filmagic Pictures and Gaïjin, and is listed as a co-production spanning 11 countries: Taiwan, France, Singapore, Poland, Greece, Japan, Germany, Brazil, South Korea, Indonesia and the Philippines.

	The Tokyo Gap-Financing Market runs as part of TIFFCOM, the content market attached to the Tokyo International Film Festival.

title: ‘The One About Matthew Perry’ Director on Gaining His Sister’s Trust, Explaining How He Died and More
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This post contains conversation about all three episodes of “The One About Matthew Perry,” now streaming on Netflix.

	At the end of
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This post contains conversation about all three episodes of “The One About Matthew Perry,” now streaming on Netflix.

	At the end of Netflix’s new docuseries “The One About Matthew Perry,” director Mary Robertson can be heard saying something off camera. “He feels very present,” Robertson softly offers to the actor’s sister Mia Perry Bowick, whose interviews serve as the centerpiece of the reflective three-episode look at the “Friends” star’s life,which was dominated by his battle with addiction.
	

	Robertson is the first to say she doesn’t believe in things she can’t see. But having spent months with the memories of Perry told through his loved ones, she admitted to one of the people who knew him best that he was more than just stories to her after this process.



	

					Matthew Perry and Mia Perry Bowick
									Courtesy of Netflix
	



	“I’m not someone who traffics in theories about the paranormal, and I don’t think I believe in UFOs, although feel free to prove me wrong,” Robertson tells Variety. “But I did feel Matthew, and I mean that in multiple senses. I felt Matthew when I was interviewing Mia, especially when we were speaking about how he would want the film to end. Her sense of Matthew is so sharp and so intimate and so present tense, and she did such an incredible job of bringing us close to her experience with him through her words and her emotion and her honesty. Not only with her voice, but through the photographs and the videos that she has. One develops a sense of Matthew’s presence, and I believe that he was present for me at the very end.”
	

	Bowick has never spoken openly about her brother’s decadeslong struggle with addiction, but now shares the full scope of Perry’s life from inside the family, including their relationship as half siblings who share the same father, actor John Bennett Perry. The series charts Perry’s meteoric rise from being a working actor to a global comedic star, thanks to “Friends” and his character Chandler Bing, and what ultimately becomes the biggest role of his life –– an advocate for addiction rehabilitation while continuously suffering from the disease himself.

	She also gives new details about private moments, including repeated visits to see him in rehab and being at his bedside in 2018 after his near-fatal colon rupture. “This is it, he is not waking up,” Bowick says in Episode 3, recalling her reaction when she first arrived at the hospital.



	

									Courtesy of Netflix
	



	Robertson commends Bowick’s candor across her two interviews, the first of which spanned two days of filming. “There were no boundaries, there were no barriers for her,” she says. At the start of the project, though, Bowick had expressed her anxiety to Robertson. “I remember when we turned on the Zoom cameras for the first meeting, Mia and her husband David looked at each other, and they inhaled and exhaled, and said, ‘We’re nervous,’” Robertson remembers. “Then I inhaled and exhaled, and I said, ‘We’re nervous too.” That was the beginning of a really beautiful connection.”

	But the series almost didn’t happen. After the release of Perry’s 2022 memoir, “Friends, Lovers, and the Big Terrible Thing,” Robertson and her Maxine Productions team reached out to his publisher and several people within his inner circle about making a documentary. They never heard back. It wasn’t until Perry’s tragic passing in 2023, from the acute effects of ketamine, that she renewed her efforts and ultimately got traction among those close to him.

	Bowick was not the first to sign on, but ultimately became the lynchpin for Robertson to feel it could be a substantial project. Also important were the voices of Perry’s closest friends, Roger Castillo and David Pressman. Robertson says Castillo signed on first, after many calls and conversations, and they flew him out to Los Angeles for the interview. Only after that did she get to plead her case to Pressman.
	



	

					Left to right: Roger Castillo, Hank Azaria, Matthew Perry, and David Pressman 
									Courtesy of Netflix
	



	“After Roger’s interview, we all had dinner with David, and Roger sat there with David and said, ‘It went really well,’” Robertson says. “I understand that Matthew’s life was harvested for content by tabloids for many, many, many years, and his friends and his loved ones were fiercely protective of Matthew. That was their trained response, and a completely understandable one. They’d never met me before, so we had to, through time and through experience, come to a place where they believed that my intentions were correct by them.”

	Robertson confirms the team did reach out to Perry’s “Friends” co-stars to participate, but “they chose not to,” she says. Still, they are present throughout the series, in archival behind-the-scenes footage and press interviews. But fans of the series will hear Bowick’s account of Perry’s being taken directly from rehab to set to film Monica (Courteney Cox) and Chandler’s wedding in Season 7; and a particularly poignant memory of his funeral, when the “Friends” cast arrived together holding hands, and stood together crying at his open casket to say goodbye.



	

									Everett Collection
	



	The documentary also features Warren Littlefield, the former entertainment president of NBC, who talks about casting Perry as Chandler and navigating, from the network’s perspective, his repeated visits to rehab while the series was filming.

	Much of Perry’s story has already been chronicled by the actor himself in his memoir. Robertson read it one sitting, and was floored by his willingness to share the depths of his addictions. “I remember the blue couch that I was sitting on, and the trees that I saw at the window as I read it,” she says. “I remember that he begins his book by saying, in essence, he should be dead. I couldn’t stop thinking about it when I was done.”

	Despite how important it was to her origins with the project, she doesn’t include anything from the memoir in the documentary, except for that opening page, which reads, “Hi, my name is Matthew, although you may know me by another name. My friends call me Matty. And I should be dead.”

	When asked why she didn’t at least try to use Perry’s darkly funny audiobook narration to give more space for his voice, she explains that the documentary is about the perspective the book can’t offer. “We wanted to craft a text that enriched what Matthew delivered through the memoir,” she says. “His memoir delivers something that, by definition, is first person, and doesn’t include the accounts of those who can describe what it was like to love someone who is completely brilliant and generous and loving, but also grappling with this enormous monster that he carried on his shoulder for most of his life. This is their account that’s missing from the memoir.”
	



	

					Roger Castillo, Matthew Perry and David Pressman 
									Courtesy of Netflix
	



	Perry does speak for himself though, through a grainy-quality but insightful interview he did with actor and friend Kevin Pollack in 2009 for the YouTube series, “Kevin Pollack’s Chat Show.” The raw footage of the interview, which Pollack granted to Robertson, winds through the documentary, giving Perry the chance to narrate his own story up to that point, which was just five years after “Friends” ended.

	The Pollack interview is different from the others that appear in the doc, including stops on the late-night circuit. It’s more casual, jovial and reflective of a life, a career and how the latter had taken over the former. Robertson says getting access to the raw, long-form footage was another moment when the potential for the documentary became clear.

	“There’s something really distinct about the quality of that interview, in that it is between two friends,” she says. “It’s not a talk show host who’s been prepped for the interview, and everyone knows exactly what they’re going to cover. They knew each other well, and they loved to make each other laugh too. Making each other laugh was their sport, so it was really transformational for our project to be able to use it.”

	But inevitably, the docuseries has to shift from looking back on Perry’s life to exploring his death, which is not uncharted territory for Robertson. In recent years, she has explored the intersection of celebrity, mental health and criminality with series like “Framing Britney Spears” for FX and “Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV” for Investigation Discovery. The former sparked a significant conversation about the nature of conservatorships and had a hand in freeing Spears from her own controversial one. The latter was an Emmy-nominated hit that let former Disney Channel and Nickelodeon child stars share their stories of abuse behind the scenes. While Robertson insists that “The One About Matthew Perry” is not an investigative piece, those two series certainly helped guide her focus here on excavating the perils of celebrity.

	“Celebrities are reflections in so many ways of our ideals,” she says. “They’re the mirror that we hold up to ourselves. They show us who and what we want to be, and who and what we are allowed to be. I believe that popular culture is tantamount to the air that we breathe. It fills our lungs and bodies, and shapes our health.”
	

	But for a subject like Perry, who so many people think they know intimately, there is still confusion surrounding his death, which ultimately led to the conviction of five people involved with supplying him the cumulatively lethal doses of ketamine.

	“As much as his final days and hours were heavily covered, there’s still some misunderstanding and mystery around what happened,” Robertson says, acknowledging the early conflicting reports of how he died and that people were indicted for their part in it. “Truth and accuracy are always our North Stars, so on some basic level, the assignment here was to render his last hours and the subsequent investigation, indictments, and sentencing with accuracy.”

	The series leans on law enforcement to help explain the details, simply because those closest to Matthew were excluded from the side of his life driven by addiction.

	“Certainly some of the people that we interviewed knew Kenny, Matthew’s assistant, who was ultimately indicted, but they were not in the house the night that Matthew passed away,” Robertson says. “They were not in the midst of these transactions, which were ultimately understood to be criminal.”

	“The One About Matthew Perry” is the mode in which Robertson wants to operate moving forward, promising more investigative portraits in the vein of “Quiet on Set” as well. She also continues to explore with Maxine Productions the branches of power and criminality, particularly with the new financial crimes-focused series, “The Wolves of Real Estate: The Alexander Brothers” for Peacock and “The Real Wolf of Wall Street” for Paramount+.

	Citing the smash-hit documentary “You Can See Everything,” Robertson says she’s excited “The One About Matthew Perry” is arriving at a time when people are actively seeking out boundary-breaking additions to the genre. While Perry’s story is told traditionally as it moves through his life, she hopes there is room to evolve the genre with renewed interest, thanks to subjects that are beloved, polarizing or a bit of both.

	“We’re entering a really interesting era of documentary filmmaking, and documentary that is roughly biographical in nature — and part of that is projects like the Elizabeth Holmes film,” Robertson says. “We’re always in dialogue with the projects that have come before us, and I think we’re at a moment of evolution in the genre, where maybe we get to be more expansive now with our understanding of what that can be.”

schema.headline: ‘The One About Matthew Perry’ Director on Gaining His Sister’s Trust, Explaining How He Died and More

title: Japanese Producers Drive Tokyo Market Growth as Exhibition Space Sells Out
description: The Tokyo International Film Festival‘s TIFFCOM market exhibition space sold out early this year, according to managing director Ikeda Kaori. More
body:
The Tokyo International Film Festival‘s TIFFCOM market exhibition space sold out early this year, according to managing director Ikeda Kaori. More Japanese producers are using the Tokyo market to find partners while projects are still in development.

	Last year’s edition drew more than 4,600 industry professionals from 46 countries and regions, and attendance rose 13%. Ikeda credits global interest in Japanese content for part of that growth.
	

	“Beyond the traditional trading of completed content, TIFFCOM has increasingly evolved into a platform for finding partners from the project development stage, leading to a significant increase in participation by Japanese producers,” Ikeda tells Variety.

	She also points to Asia, which is now one of the world’s largest markets. Governments across the region are actively backing their content industries, she says.

	This year’s Tokyo IP Market has grown to 10 participating IP holders and adds new categories, toys among them. The pitch event has also changed format. Each company now gives a focused pitch on its flagship IP.

	The changes come after the market’s expansion to the Cannes Film Market this year, where more than 700 people registered for its pitches, panels and related programs. The audience was mostly from Europe and Hollywood. Ikeda says the IP holders who took part held a run of meetings with partners they rarely get to see in person. An initiative proposed by the Cannes market also set up matchmaking with the XR sector.

	Overseas interest goes beyond the obvious hits. “IPs with an established audience, including ‘One Piece’ and ‘Super Mario,’ are undoubtedly attractive. On the other hand, Japan still possesses a great number of outstanding original works with strong potential for screen adaptations and remakes, and Tokyo IP Market is designed as the platform to discover them,” Ikeda says. Many producers want to adapt or distribute distinctive stories that are not yet well known, she adds, and each market has its own scale and audience.
	

	The Tokyo Gap-Financing Market (TGFM) has 24 live-action and animation projects this year. It has also teamed with Canadian genre outfit Frontières. Ikeda says Japan, Thailand and Indonesia stand out in Asia for genre films such as horror and thrillers.

	“Horror in particular is often deeply rooted in local culture and traditions, making it naturally unique while offering exceptional entertainment value,” she says. TGFM wants the genre focus to widen the mix of projects and filmmakers at the market. It also hopes to give Asian projects a route into North America.

	The market already has results to show. Two projects developed through TGFM are at this year’s Tokyo International Film Festival. “The Violinist,” which took part in 2023, won the top prize at Annecy this year. Ikeda understands that the Italian financing on “The Violinist” and the Thai financing on “Four Seasons in Java” both came from connections made at TIFFCOM.

	“As a gap financing market, the primary goal is the completion of the film, and being selected for film festivals is a major initial bonus,” she says.

	Japanese broadcasters feature prominently in this year’s conference program. TBS will present its partnership with Legendary Entertainment and the worldwide rollout of “Sasuke,” known overseas as “Ninja Warrior.” Nippon TV will discuss its global strategy, including a drama co-produced with South Korea. In a session run by the Broadcast Program Export Association of Japan (BEAJ), TV Tokyo will present a case study on taking IP overseas through experiential exhibitions.

	“While terrestrial TV remains strong in Japan, all broadcasters are actively accelerating their global initiatives. Japanese broadcasters have always been a treasure trove of powerful IP, including formats and dramas,” Ikeda says.

	For anime studios looking at international partnerships, she sees the biggest obstacle as hesitation that comes from a lack of international experience. “While language and cultural differences exist, the core issue is a shortage of talent with experience in international co-production, which in turn leads to a lack of established networks. On the flip side, however, this means there is immense room for growth,” she says. TIFFCOM is hosting a conference on international anime co-production this year, where experts will cover project structuring and financing.
	

	Short-form drama is also growing fast in Japan. Participation from AI and data analytics companies is rising steadily, and another conference looks at trends in Japanese content through data. AGBO is giving this year’s keynote.

	“In such a fast-moving environment, what holds true value is first-hand insights into how AI is being used at the cutting edge,” Ikeda says. TIFFCOM is also keen to explore using AI in its own operations.

	The program also includes Taiwanese project showcases, Chinese content presentations and co-production discussions involving Brazil, Canada and Japan. Ikeda doesn’t see a conflict between TIFFCOM’s role as the main marketplace for Japanese content and its goal of becoming a hub for Asia. She calls them two essential pillars.

	“Southeast Asia in particular is experiencing rapid growth in both economic strength and production capabilities, alongside rising demand for Japanese content. As buyers in each country grow their domestic businesses, their opportunities to acquire Japanese content will also expand,” she says.

	Ikeda doesn’t want to narrow TIFFCOM to a single next area. Instead, she wants it to keep adapting as trends and formats change, and to add partnerships with other markets and events along the lines of the Cannes collaboration.

	“The content industry five years from now holds so much potential that it cannot yet be defined – and that is precisely what makes it so exciting,” she says.

title: Jafar Panahi Now Faces a Five-Year Prison Term in New Ruling on Top of His Previous One-Year Conviction
description: Cannes Palme d’Or-winning Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi – who was facing a one-year prison sentence – has now been sentenced by a Tehran Revolutio
body:
Cannes Palme d’Or-winning Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi – who was facing a one-year prison sentence – has now been sentenced by a Tehran Revolutionary Court to five years and one month in jail in a separate ruling, according to the Emtedad News Agency, an online Iranian reformist media outlet.

	Panahi’s lawyer Mostafa Nili told Emtedad that the court has now sentenced his client in absentia to five years and one month of imprisonment – though implementation of both rulings is discretionary – and issued an order for the confiscation of Panahi’s assets, plus a two-year ban on using social media a two-year travel ban. It is unclear what the charges against Panahi are in this case.
	

	The lawyer said that after Panahi’s bank accounts were suddenly frozen last week, he went to the prosecutor’s Tehran office with his client and learned of the verdict which has been issued in absentia. According to Nili, the case file stated that Panahi was living outside Iran, though the director had returned to Iran on March 30, 2026 shortly after the ceremony for the 98th Academy Awards, in which his latest film ”It Was Just an Accident” made it to the nomination stage as France’s candidate in the Best International Feature Film Category.

	Over the past two decades, Panahi has had frequent run-ins with the Iranian authorities.

	In 2010, the revered auteur — known globally also for other prize-winning works such as “The Circle,” “Offside,” “This is Not a Film,” “Taxi” and “No Bears” — was banned from making movies, speaking to the press and traveling, though he surreptitiously kept making them anyway.
	

	In 2022, Panahi was arrested in connection with protests by a group of filmmakers but was released about seven months later.

	The ban was lifted in April 2023, and Iranian authorities allowed Panahi to travel to Cannes to launch “It Was Just an Accident.” Panahi subsequently traveled widely to promote the drama, which centers around an outpouring of strong feelings by a group of former prisoners toward a torturous guard and stems from his incarceration.

	But he returned to Iran despite the fact that, at that point, he faced a one-year prison sentence in his home country and a climate of escalating tension that made his return very risky.

	“I am the kind of person who needs to be in his country,” Panahi told Variety. “I need to breathe there and work there. And even if they want to go ahead with that prison sentence, they can go ahead. Nothing will change my mind about going back.”

schema.headline: Jafar Panahi Now Faces a Five-Year Prison Term in New Ruling on Top of His Previous One-Year Conviction

title: Barry Keoghan Undergoes Skin-Tightening Cosmetic Treatment in Video Posted Months After He Called Out Online Abuse Over ‘How I Look’
description: Barry Keoghan is making headlines for appearing in a new social media video shared by U.K. celebrity facial expert and Dermaspa founder Nilam Holme
body:
Barry Keoghan is making headlines for appearing in a new social media video shared by U.K. celebrity facial expert and Dermaspa founder Nilam Holmes, who posted a behind-the-scenes look at the Oscar nominee’s Xerf treatment. Per Dermaspa’s website, Xerf forgoes injections and uses radio-frequency technology to tighten the skin and renew collagen. The treatment costs around $3,500 for a face and neck session. 

	“I’ve been working with Barry for a while now, looking after his skin through different movies, campaigns and projects and the trust he places in me means a lot,” Holmes wrote in a caption accompanying the video. “His skin has really improved over the last few years and he looks great. Today we did his [second Xerf] skin-tightening treatment. I was running late filming some Xerf content, so rather than make me rush what I was doing, he offered to let me film him having it.”
	

	Keoghan narrates the video, saying: “I’ve been hearing a lot about it, and Nilam is very excited about it, and she’s great at what she does. I really mean that, and again, every time I come in, it’s very relaxing and therapeutic. I feel better about myself, I look better. I think it’s important to look after yourself inside and outside.”

	As seen on Holmes’ social media pages, her other clients who have undergone Xerf treatment include Chris Appleton, Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, Joe Alwyn and Nicole Scherzinger. She’s also worked with Pink and Joe Alwyn and has posted regularly about treating Keoghan in the past, giving him facials before various photo shoots.

	“Working on multiple projects at a time; movies, campaigns, interviews, press and philanthropy projects means unstructured routine, travel, make up, and disrupted sleep patterns, which all take a toll on the skin,” Holmes posted in March 2025 about treating Keoghan for his Wonderland magazine cover. “So we have regular skin sessions which consist of fixing up problematic skin, calming down inflammation, maintaining the skin when it’s great and trying to get that healthy, rested look. On top of that Barry is like a little student for me. Passionate about everything, he likes to know everything about everything which I love and he brings the fun when he visits.”
	

	Earlier this year, Keoghan went viral for telling SiriusXM’s “The Morning Mash Up” that the online “abuse” about his appearance had gotten so bad that he no longer wanted to “go outside.”

	“There’s a lot of hate online,” Keoghan explained at the time. “There’s a lot of abuse of how I look, and it’s kind of past the point of — you know, everyone goes through that… but it’s made me shy away. It’s made me really go inside myself, not want to attend places, not want to go outside. I say this being absolute pure and honest to you. It’s becoming a problem.”

	Keoghan noted that he removed himself from social media to avoid nasty comments about himself, but occasionally, after a premiere or event, he would go online to see “how he’s received.” Unfortunately, he said most of the time, the reaction is “not nice.”

schema.headline: Barry Keoghan Undergoes Skin-Tightening Cosmetic Treatment in Video Posted Months After He Called Out Online Abuse Over ‘How I Look’

title: ‘Altadena: One Fire After Another’ Documentary Set by Former ’60 Minutes’ Producers (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Climate journalist Bill McKibben and executive producer and former “60 Minutes” producer David Gelber have teamed up to create “Altadena: One Fire
body:
Climate journalist Bill McKibben and executive producer and former “60 Minutes” producer David Gelber have teamed up to create “Altadena: One Fire After Another,” a documentary chronicling the aftermath of the 2025 Eaton Fire in Los Angeles. The film follows Altadena residents as they confront the challenges of rebuilding their homes, preserving their community and navigating the long road to recovery.

	While much of the initial coverage focused on the night the fire erupted, the documentary picks up the story more than a year later.
	

	“The fire was only the beginning of the story,” Gelber said in a statement. “We wanted to understand what happens after the television cameras leave, when families are left to rebuild not only their homes but also their lives and sense of community. Altadena’s story is deeply personal, but it’s also a window into questions communities across the country are increasingly facing.”



	

	



	The film features interviews with Altadena residents sharing personal stories along with conversations with professionals on climate, economics and public policy.

	“We’ve become accustomed to covering disasters as breaking news. What’s far less visible is what comes next. This film is about the months and years after a catastrophe, when the real consequences begin to unfold,” McKibben said in a statement. “I hope people take away from the documentary the fact that this is not a random tragedy in any way; rather, it’s caused by a particular set of players doing a particular thing.”



	

	



	The film is produced and directed by Jonathan Scheinberg and produced and edited by Vanessa Gould. The documentary team’s credits include “60 Minutes,” “Years of Living Dangerously,” ABC News, CBS News, HBO, CNN, The New York Times and National Geographic. “Altadena: One Fire After Another” is currently in post-production, with the filmmakers currently evaluating distribution opportunities.

title: ’60 Minutes’ Audience Sinks to Surprising Low Without Football
description: It’s not surprising to see ratings at “60 Minutes” slump when CBS doesn’t air a strong football game before the start of the show. But the program’
body:
It’s not surprising to see ratings at “60 Minutes” slump when CBS doesn’t air a strong football game before the start of the show. But the program’s performance on Sunday, which lacked exactly that kind of NFL lead-in, is alarming nonetheless.

	The fifth episode of this season’s cycle of the venerable CBS newsmagazine drew only 5.64 million viewers, one of the smallest audiences for the program in years, according to data from Nielsen. The show captured a mere 558,000 among viewers between 25 and 54, the demographic coveted most by advertisers in news programming. 
	

	Since 2000, a sixth episode of “60 Minutes” has never failed to capture less than seven million viewers overall and less than one million viewers in the advertiser category.

	CBS News declined to make executives available for comment, and the network had not released the Nielsen data itself publicly as of Tuesday evening. The Nielsen numbers were confirmed by four people familiar with the information. For the night, “60 Minutes” was the second-most-watched non-sports program on broadcast TV, behind CBS dramas “Tracker” and “Marshals.” Typically, “60 Minutes” finishes first in that category.

	Such numbers may be cause for consternation at CBS News, the CBS television network and corporate parent Skydance. “60 Minutes” has long stood as one of the most-watched programs on TV that isn’t tied to sports, and is supposed to funnel viewers from the NFL into the rest of the CBS Sunday primetime lineup. Compared to the year-earlier telecast of the newsmagazine, which had a more robust football lead-in, Sunday’s telecast of “60 Minutes” fell 60% in overall viewership and a whopping 81% among viewers between 25 and 54.  
	

	CBS News remains under intense pressure to demonstrate stability at the program, which was overhauled in chaotic fashion at the end of last season, despite mustering a notable 9% uptick in overall viewership. Bari Weiss, CBS News’ editor in chief, ousted Tanya Simon, an executive producer with years of history working at the show, in favor of Nick Bilton, a journalist and screenwriter with less formal TV experience. Also pushed out were correspondents Scott Pelley, Cecilia Vega and Sharyn Alfonsi. Anderson Cooper left of his own volition following the end of his contract. Their replacements, which include Ross Douthat and contributors like Ariel Levy and Sebastian Junger, have top-shelf backgrounds, but also little experience working on a weekly TV program that emphasizes long-form enterprise journalism.

	Sunday’s telecast faced competition from a late football game on Fox.

	The program featured a probe into the Trump administration’s efforts to deport people to countries where they have no ties, and the show’s investigation revealed how some deportees are being subsequently forced back to the nations they originally fled. The segment echoed one from last season during which correspondent Alfonsi examined the deportation of some migrants to harsh prisons in El Salvador, a story that generated controversy because Weiss asked it for it be held at a late stage in production.  The show also featured interviews with Colorado Governor Jared Polis and Tina Peters, a top election official whose sentence tied to a conviction of breaching her county’s election system he commuted.

schema.headline: ’60 Minutes’ Audience Sinks to Surprising Low Without Football

title: Elmo Is Going as Meryl Streep’s Evil Fashion Editor Miranda Priestly for Halloween This Year
description:
This Halloween, “Sesame Street‘s” beloved furry red monster is trading crayons for couture. 

	In a somewhat unexpected cultural crossover, Elmo fo
body:
This Halloween, “Sesame Street‘s” beloved furry red monster is trading crayons for couture. 

	In a somewhat unexpected cultural crossover, Elmo for Halloween 2026 is dressing as fashion magazine editor-in-chief-from-hell Miranda Priestly, archly portrayed in the “The Devil Wears Prada” movies by Oscar-winner Meryl Streep.

	“Guess who Elmo is?” he says in a video released by “Sesame Street,” before revealing his Miranda Priestly look.
	

	In the video, a sentient pumpkin strolls in front of Elmo, prompting him to crack in character as Priestly: “Pumpkins. For fall. How groundbreaking.” Then Cookie Monster appears, prompting Elmo to snark about Cookie’s blue fur color: “Well, it’s not cerulean. But, it works.” To which Cookie Monster responds: “Uh, thanks? Me think?”

	Watch the video below — which will certainly fly right over the heads of Elmo’s preschool fans.

	In years past, Elmo in different “Sesame Street” segments has dressed for Halloween as a spaceman known as “Galactic Stan,” as well as a pirate and a witch. Meanwhile, Elmo himself continues to be a popular Halloween costume selection for kids and adults alike.

	Streep starred in the original 2006 “The Devil Wear’s Prada” movie alongside Anne Hathaway, Emily Blunt and Stanley Tucci. The movie is based on the novel of the same name by Lauren Weisberger, who once worked at Vogue and modeled the Miranda character on real-life fashion editor Anna Wintour. The quartet of actors reprised their characters in this year’s sequel, “The Devil Wears Prada 2,” from 20th Century Studios.

schema.headline: Elmo Is Going as Meryl Streep’s Evil Fashion Editor Miranda Priestly for Halloween This Year

title: Japan Must Follow Hollywood’s Distribution Playbook, Says Tokyo Market Chief Shiina Yasushi, Who Eyes Major Expansion by 2030
description: Japan’s entertainment business has to adopt the model that made Hollywood studios global players if the country wants to reach its content export t
body:
Japan’s entertainment business has to adopt the model that made Hollywood studios global players if the country wants to reach its content export targets, according to Shiina Yasushi, CEO of TIFFCOM, the Tokyo International Film Festival‘s content market now heading into its 23rd edition.

	The Japanese government has set a target of JPY20 trillion ($126.6 billion) in overseas content sales by 2033, and expects anime to bring in JPY6 trillion ($38 billion) of that. Shiina argues that looking abroad won’t be enough without a change in how Japanese companies operate.
	

	“Historically, Japanese companies have often licensed content rights abroad and left local distribution and marketing to their licensees. Going forward, companies should retain ownership of their IP, be actively involved in international distribution, and maximize the revenue generated from their properties,” Shiina tells Variety.

	He points out that Hollywood studios reached global scale by setting up their own distribution operations country by country and dealing with each market directly. Japan should take the same route, he says. With that base in place, a property can then be spread across film, games, streaming and merchandise. Shiina sees this as the shift to the “IP-driven industry” the government has called for.

	Japanese companies have begun rethinking how they handle IP. TBS is working with Legendary Entertainment, Nippon TV is expanding internationally and publishers are looking at overseas adaptations. Shiina says a fundamental shift is under way. “In the past, the very concept of the long-term value of IP was not widely considered,” he says. Talent agencies have also started paying attention to IP, he adds, because the IP a performer worked on can live on long after they retire.
	

	According to Shiina, the market itself has changed most in who attends. TIFFCOM used to be mainly a place where international sales agents traded finished content. Once producers arrived, it became a more creative market. Streamers now attend next to film and TV companies, and the IP holders on the floor include anime studios, publishers, game companies and toy makers.

	The Tokyo Gap-Financing Market (TGFM) is now big enough to build programs around specific regions and genres, Shiina says. Alongside its Asian focus, it has a collaboration with Italy and, this year, a partnership with Canada’s genre outfit Frontières. When TGFM started, it simply picked projects that met its eligibility rules.

	The aim is to make Tokyo a key stop for developing and financing projects, as well as for selling finished ones. “While traditional markets centered on sellers and buyers, our vision is a marketplace where everyone involved in production comes together – from producers, directors, and screenwriters to studios and investors providing capital,” Shiina says.

	Taking the Tokyo IP Market to the Cannes Film Market raised TIFFCOM’s profile. Even so, Shiina says the goal isn’t simply to repeat that move at other overseas markets. The priority is still getting international professionals to come to Japan.

	“Japan possesses such compelling IP that creators and producers around the world want to collaborate with us. By coming to Japan, international partners can engage in direct, face-to-face dialogue with creators – including original authors, directors, and screenwriters,” he says.

	At Cannes, Japan was Country of Honor. Its delegation included sales executives, directors, producers, studios and senior company leaders. Because the program featured anime studios and IP as well as live-action, publishers went too. For Shiina, the biggest result was a change in attitude. Japanese executives who used to see festival markets only as places to buy and sell finished films found out they could take part themselves.

	He wants to keep that from being a one-time event. “If Cannes was the first step, this edition of Tokyo represents the second step, and we are still just at the beginning. By sustaining this virtuous cycle, we aim to build a lasting, sustainable business,” Shiina says.
	

	TIFFCOM’s technology keynote this year features AGBO executives speaking about AI and storytelling. Shiina won’t predict which part of the business AI will change first. He is sure, though, that it will reshape production by lowering costs and shortening turnaround. Rights are his main worry, and he says the whole industry needs to work on frameworks for them.

	“The critical priority is how to protect creators. This year’s keynote features AGBO – a studio founded by film directors – speaking on how to leverage AI and technology in a creator-led manner, which I believe is precisely the topic the industry wants to hear right now,” he says.

	Shiina doesn’t think Japan can settle the AI question alone. Both the technology and the rights involved cross borders, and he says opting out of AI is no longer realistic.

	On anime’s long-running problems with costs, working conditions and creators’ share of profits, Shiina says things are getting better, though slowly. He cites work-style reforms, a new law protecting freelancers, and joint government and industry efforts on working conditions. Studios are also starting to keep their IP and build their own businesses instead of working only as subcontractors, and live-action producers are doing the same. “I believe anime is leading the way worldwide, with live-action following in its footsteps,” he says.

	Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market and Hong Kong FilMart are also chasing international growth. Shiina says a market should be judged on quality, not numbers. “When industry professionals plan their annual calendars, Tokyo remains an unmissable destination because it allows them to connect directly with Japanese rights holders and creators,” he says. Getting more Japanese companies to take part is the key, he adds, because international attendance follows Japanese participation.

	Looking ahead, Shiina wants to expand TIFFCOM’s capacity across its whole operation, not just its floor space. “By around 2030, including venue expansion, we envision growing TIFFCOM into a significantly expanded marketplace,” he says.

schema.headline: Japan Must Follow Hollywood’s Distribution Playbook, Says Tokyo Market Chief Shiina Yasushi, Who Eyes Major Expansion by 2030

title: Judge Warns Against Outing Anonymous Celebrity Amid Sex Scandal, Suicide Fears
description:
Anonymous Celeb
                          Judge Warns Public Not to Reveal Man's Identity ...
body:
Anonymous Celeb
                          Judge Warns Public Not to Reveal Man's Identity ...
                          Amid Sex Misconduct Claims
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 27, 2026
                            3:30 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A judge is putting the public on notice ... warning people to stop trying to identify the mystery celebrity fighting to keep serious sexual misconduct allegations under wraps ... or they could wind up behind bars themselves.
      
    
            Judge Matthew Nicklin issued the warning during a hearing in London's High Court Tuesday ... after online sleuths began tossing around names in an attempt to unmask the famous man, who's only been identified in court as "PPT."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            According to The Independent, the judge acknowledged the growing speculation ... but made it clear that even if a name is being widely circulated online, that doesn't make it fair game to publish.
      

            He warned that reporting restrictions remain in effect ... meaning the press and public are barred from identifying the man, including on social media.
      
    
            And the consequences could be serious ... anyone who violates the court order could face contempt proceedings, potentially carrying up to 2 years in prison or a fine.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Nicklin also pointed out that multiple people have already been named in online speculation ... reminding everyone that repeating rumors doesn't make them facts.
      
    
            As we previously reported, the unnamed celebrity is suing ITN and The Guardian to prevent them from publishing allegations that he used his fame to pursue girls and young women over several years, including an alleged sexual offense. He denies the accusations.
      
    
            His lawyers have warned publication could put his life at risk ... with the court previously hearing he'd attempted suicide twice in recent months and remains seriously ill.
      
    
            The news outlets are fighting his effort to block their reporting ... arguing the allegations are a matter of public interest.
      
    
            For now, the celebrity's identity remains protected ... and the judge is making sure everyone knows the rules apply to social media sleuths, too.
      
    
            If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, help is available. Call or text 988 or chat 988lifeline.org.
